title: A Crying Toddler. An Unexpected Response.
context: A parent remembers a subway ride in Korea: a crying toddler, an older couple nearby, and a small surprise.
question: What happened next?

options.text: Took out toys to help calm the child.
Offered a few reassuring words to the parent.

reveal: The couple took out toys they had with them to help calm the child. A small thing to try when a journey gets difficult.
insight: Sometimes a little help looks like whatever you happen to have with you.

title: Same Town. A Completely Different Evening.
context: A Korean coastal town. Packed restaurants on the weekend. Come back another evening, and the mood changes completely.
question: Which evening brought the quieter mood?
reveal: Monday night: barely anyone in the restaurants, and a much slower pace. The town’s name had slipped from memory; the contrast had not.
insight: A place on your itinerary might have more than one mood.

title: Can a Busy City Feel Peaceful?
context: A late walk. Lights still on. Somewhere to go. For one night owl, Seoul felt like home.
question: Which evening would help you unwind?

options.text: Quiet streets and an early night.
A late walk with somewhere still open.

revealHeadline: Their kind of quiet had the lights on.
reveal: Places to go late at night felt comforting rather than overwhelming. The appeal was Seoul’s energy—a feeling the writer also recognized could exist in other big cities.
insight: What feels restful to you: fewer things happening, or more possibilities?

title: Great Food. Great Transit. Still Not Your City?
context: Great food. Easy transport. And still, Seoul did not quite click for one visitor.
question: What most shapes whether a city feels right to you?

options.text: How convenient it is to explore and eat well.
How its streets and neighborhoods make me feel.

revealHeadline: A good trip can come with mixed feelings.
reveal: A great barbecue meal. An enjoyable mountain outing. But around the accommodation, the buildings felt close and confining. Same trip, different feelings.
insight: You can enjoy parts of a city without falling in love with the whole place.

title: A Wedding Invite from Someone You Barely Know
context: Back in Korea after years abroad, someone gets a wedding invitation from a coworker they barely know. Included: bank details for a congratulatory gift.
question: Which response would feel more natural to you?

options.text: Send a small gift as a friendly gesture.

reveal: The awkward part was closeness: what feels right when you barely know each other? The story leaves the coworker’s intention—and the eventual decision—open.
insight: Where would you draw the line between a friendly gesture and a social obligation?
